text: Double/debiased machine learning removes the bias from regularization and overfitting in the nuisance estimates by combining Neyman-orthogonal scores with cross-fitting.

Chernozhukov et al. (2018, Table 2, Panel B) report partially linear DML estimates of the effect of 401(k) eligibility on net financial assets between $7,717 (lasso, 2-fold) and $9,247 (random forest, 5-fold) across seven nuisance learners.

With 5-fold cross-fitting and random forests, the published partially linear estimate is $9,247 with a split-adjusted standard error of 1,328 (median standard error 1,295) (Chernozhukov et al. 2018, Table 2, Panel B).
Without controls, the estimated difference in net financial assets by 401(k) eligibility is $19,559 with a standard error of 1,413.

The published estimates use the DML2 estimator with 2-fold and 5-fold cross-fitting, repeated over 100 random sample splits, and aggregate point estimates and standard errors across splits with the median method.

The outcome is net financial assets, the treatment is eligibility to enroll in a 401(k) plan, and the controls are age, income, family size, years of education, and indicators for marriage, two-earner household, defined-benefit pension, IRA participation and home ownership.
Chernozhukov et al. (2018) use the same 1991 SIPP data as Chernozhukov and Hansen (2004).
The authors' public replication repository distributes the data as sipp1991.dta, and its 401(k) script states that the sample selection and variable construction follow Abadie (2003).
The SIPP 1991 extract contains 9,915 households.

As summarized by Chernozhukov et al. (2018), Poterba, Venti and Wise argue that 401(k) eligibility can be treated as exogenous after conditioning on income and other job-related observables, because around the time 401(k) plans became available workers were unlikely to choose employers on that basis.
Poterba, Venti and Wise (1995), using the 1984, 1987 and 1991 SIPP, find little evidence that 401(k) contributions substitute for other personal saving.

Chernozhukov and Hansen (2004) use 401(k) eligibility as an instrument for participation and find positive, significant quantile effects of participation on net financial assets across the distribution.
DoubleML implements the DML framework of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) as open-source software in Python and R.

The 401(k) partially linear model has been re-estimated with DML in software papers and documentation: ddml in Stata reports $9,748.79 (SE 1,331.36) with short-stacking, 4 folds and one resample; the DoubleML Python example reports $8,909.63 (SE 1,321.82) with random forests and 3 folds; Chernozhukov et al. (2026) report $9,002 (SE 1,394) with random forests.
An earlier run of the same exercise by the same authors gave a median 5-fold random-forest partially linear estimate of $9,252 (SE 1,400), within $5 of the 2018 published value.

Among the published and online re-analyses of the 401(k) data that we read, none reproduces Table 2, Panel B of Chernozhukov et al. (2018) cell by cell under its protocol (2- and 5-fold cross-fitting, 100 splits, median aggregation) with a side-by-side comparison; they use other fold counts, a single split, other estimators or other outcomes, or use the data only to calibrate simulations.

When rlasso is called with post = FALSE and a penalty list supplying c = 1.1 (as in the authors' code), hdm 0.2.0, 0.3.1 and 0.3.2 reset the penalty constant to 0.5 and hdm 0.2.3 keeps 1.1; hdm 0.1.0 also resets c to 0.5 but computes lambda0 as 2c sqrt(n) sqrt(2 log(2p log(n)/gamma)), which at the study's n and p = 275 equals the qnorm-based formula with an effective c of about 0.62, so c = 0.5 in the qnorm formula does not reproduce hdm 0.1.0. rlassologit keeps the supplied c = 1.1 in all five CRAN versions.
The Table 2 estimates published in 2018 first appear in arXiv:1608.00060v5 (21 June 2017); version 4 (30 December 2016) reports an earlier run.

H2 cell verdict, random forest 2-fold: pass (testable cell; |diff| = $52 <= tolerance $438). In the plan's decision rule (design.decision_rules.H2) a pass means no shift larger than the cell's 80%-power detectable shift ($569) was detected; it never means the estimates are identical, and a shift up to that size is not ruled out (hypotheses[1] names the tolerance instead; see h2-decision). The forest port failed the pre-gate check (check-learner-ports): the Python forest's theta was $216 lower than randomForest's (synthetic-outcome dollars, SE $9) at this 2-fold training size. This cell's difference (-$52) does not show that shift, but it lies below the detectable shift ($569), so the pass does not show that the forest port reproduces randomForest; it does not rule out a shift of that size either.

H2 cell verdict, random forest 5-fold: pass (testable cell; |diff| = $206 <= tolerance $287). In the plan's decision rule (design.decision_rules.H2) a pass means no shift larger than the cell's 80%-power detectable shift ($373) was detected; it never means the estimates are identical, and a shift up to that size is not ruled out (hypotheses[1] names the tolerance instead; see h2-decision). This cell's difference (-$206) is close to the forest port shift measured before the gate (-$216 in synthetic-outcome dollars, SE $9; the forest port check failed), and it lies below the detectable shift ($373): the pass does not show that the forest port reproduces randomForest, and the cell sits where the known port deviation predicts. That shift was measured at the 2-fold training size only; the 2-fold cell does not show it (difference -$52, see plr-forest-2fold-h2), and neither forest cell can tell a zero shift from a -$216 shift.

H2 holds under design.decision_rules.H2: 0 of 10 cells are outside their tolerance and 8 of 8 testable cells are inside; the two lasso cells are inside but not testable at this resolution and are not counted as passes. Meaning of a pass: the plan's decision rule (design.decision_rules.H2), which governs the verdict, says a pass means 'no shift larger than the cell's 80%-power detectable shift was detected', never 'identical'. hypotheses[1] words it as 'no shift larger than the stated per-cell tolerance was detected'. The two texts apply the same test (|diff| <= tolerance) and differ only in the shift they name: the tolerance is the shift detected about half the time, the 80%-power detectable shift (about 1.30 x the tolerance) the one detected 80% of the time. We use the decision rule's wording: shifts below a cell's detectable shift are not ruled out. The 5-fold forest cell passes with a difference close to the forest port deviation measured before the gate (claim plr-forest-5fold-h2).

The published lasso adjusted SEs are not reproduced: replicated vs published adjusted SE 1,377 vs 1,749 (ratio 0.79) at 2-fold and 1,309 vs 1,558 (ratio 0.84) at 5-fold, while the bracketed SEs match within $2. The adjusted-SE gap comes from the split-to-split spread (1.4826 x MAD of the per-split estimates): $354 vs $1,656 implied by the published SEs at 2-fold, $190 vs $1,278 at 5-fold, 4.7 and 6.7 times narrower; for the other learners the ratio is 1.2-1.7. These are the only published estimates or SEs that the replication misses by more than 15%. Why the replicated lasso spread is narrower is not tested by any run. Consequence: a lasso median that matches the published one to within $16 while its split distribution is several times narrower is weak evidence that the port behaves like the authors' lasso on net_tfa. The lasso agreement is therefore read only as 'inside the tolerance, not testable at this resolution', never as a reproduction.
